attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter, presented in his own voice.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the carve-out for the two labs' compute spend. Reading 'these companies' as Google, Microsoft and Amazon fits the heading just before it.

contract.note: The speaker's next sentence says AI is not 'boosting other product categories', so asking whether AI contributes materially is an ordinary reading. Using the April–June 2026 quarter is reasonable. Counting product attributions in company disclosures matches his own test: they would 'tell you specifically'.

evidence.note: Alphabet's Q2 2026 letter names Gemini Enterprise as one of the strongest sources of Cloud growth and lists named enterprise customers. This is AI growth beyond the two labs' compute spend. It is management's own attribution.

Microsoft's FY26 Q4 remarks say Copilot, among its premium offerings, drove M365 revenue-per-user growth, with paid seats now over 30 million. These are customer product sales, outside the excluded compute spend. It is management's own attribution.

reviews.rationale: The contract is met if product-specific evidence shows AI adding materially to growth at one or more of the companies. Google (Gemini Enterprise) and Microsoft (Copilot) both name a specific AI product, its customers, and its role in Q2 2026 growth. Both sources are management's own claims, not independent proof of causation, and Amazon was not examined. Still, they do the 'tell you specifically' that the speaker said would never happen.

attribution.note: Zitron's own concluding words in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: Treating this as a statement about current exit prospects is right. 'Needs a miracle' is emphasis. 'Few signs' has no threshold, and 'these companies' could mean all AI startups or only the frontier labs.

contract.note: The plain reading of scarce exit routes is fair. The result depends on two choices the speaker did not supply: which companies 'these companies' means, and what counts as 'few'. The contract also says a handful of examples cannot by themselves disprove 'few signs'.

evidence.note: Anthropic, a central company in the post, announced a confidential draft S-1 on June 1, 2026. That is a concrete sign of an IPO route, but not a completed listing.
Cerebras completed its Nasdaq listing in May 2026, an AI exit within the target quarter. It is one example. A 2025 date in the release looks like a typo.
Q2 venture exits set records, with Cerebras among the largest listings. The data covers all venture-backed companies, not AI specifically.
A secondary summary: exit value was concentrated in SpaceX. It also mentions the Cursor acquisition and reported IPO filings by both OpenAI and Anthropic. Covers all US venture.

reviews.rationale: The evidence leans against the claim: Anthropic filed for an IPO, Cerebras listed, Cursor was acquired, and venture exits hit records in Q2 2026. But the contract asks for an AI-specific exit record with a comparison population, and says a few examples cannot disprove 'few signs'. The packet has no AI-specific measure across the sector, so the sweeping claim is not settled either way.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: Firm, unhedged wording that implies NVIDIA will fall short of the quoted FY2028 and 2029 analyst figures. Treating it as a forecast with those targets is faithful.

contract.note: Testing realized revenue against the two quoted targets is an ordinary reading. The mixed case for one target missed is reasonable. The contract correctly says a revenue miss alone would not prove the funding explanation.

evidence.note: Revenue for NVIDIA's FY2027 Q2 quarter was $96.2B. That is an earlier period, and the contract says quarterly revenue cannot stand in for the annual targets.

reviews.rationale: Neither FY2028 nor FY2029 had ended by the 2026-10-28 evaluation date, and no event meets the early-resolution rule. Quarterly FY2027 results are context only. The forecast cannot be scored yet.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, in his voice, answering a view he attributes to others.

semantics.note: 'They did, and there wasn't' answers the idea that smart people wouldn't spend that money without a massive return. So the claim is that the AI spending produced no massive return. 'Massive' and 'didn't work' are not quantified.

contract.note: Reading 'return' as realized financial return relative to AI investment, as of the latest quarter, is a fair and ordinary reading of 'massive return'.

evidence.note: Microsoft Cloud revenue grew 27%, and contracted future revenue (RPO) rose to $678B. Neither isolates AI or measures return on investment, and the figures cover only one of the four hyperscalers.

reviews.rationale: The contract needs matched estimates of AI investment against attributable returns across the hyperscalers. The packet has only Microsoft's broad cloud revenue, which neither supports nor contradicts the claim. There is no threshold for 'massive', and no AI return calculation was found.
